As a matter of fact, I am convinced that we could have

thore.
On Thursday I called on Sir Archibald Clark Kerr, the Brit-
1sh Ambassador to China, and he sent a rush message to the Governor
1 bongkong, requesting
permission for CHAC to come in that night.
later he got a reply irom the Governor authorizing two ilights be-

permission to make more flights the following night but got no reply.
At 4 o'clock that afternoon, two of our DC-3's, flown by Pilots
McDonaid and Higgs, left Chungking for Hongkong to make the two
flights authorized. About one hour out of Hongkong they recoived a
message from Moss telling them that arrangements had been cancelled
and instructing them not to come to Hongkong.
No reason was given.
McDonald and Higgs then changed their course to Namyung, where thes
landed and picked up members of our staff left there on previous
flights cut of longkong and returned to Chungking.
That was our
last effort to get into Hongkong.
On Thursday we got word the Japanese had raided Nanyung
heavily and had repeatedly machine-gunned our DC-3 at low altitudes•"
The engines were ruined and so were the props.
Most of the instru-
ments were shot to pieces, the tires, control lines, hydraulic lines,
landing gear and gas tanks. We have dismantled it and got it off
the field several miles.
We plan to bulld sneds over the fusilage
and wings and rebuild it. It will take a long time and we must have
lots of parts from the States. We can do the rebuilding in five or
six months. I can't even guess when we can get the parts from the
States, but one of these days me will have it back in service.
I would like to say here that I have since criticized my-
selt severely for leaving Schafer. I feel very badly about it, but
at the time it seemed the best thing to do and there did not seem to
be any increased danger.
Schafer's conduct throughout was splendid.
He is a good man and could handle the situation very well. I felt
perfectly satisfied in leaving everything to him, but I am sorry
now that I did.
For the last three days we have made flights every evening
to Namyung and back, bringing out supplies which have been evacuated
out of Hongkong. We are resuming our schedules to the extent of
three times per week from Chungking to Kunming to Lashio and one of
these trips to Lashio continues to Calcutta.

Chungking
December 17, 1941
HI. Ho M. Bixby
Pan American Airways, Inc.
Chrysler Building
New
York, N.Y., U.S.A.
Dear ir. Bixby:
On Monday morning, December 8th, Just before breakfast,
I was called to the telephone by Captain Ralph, who informed me
he had a message from Manile instructing him not to take off the
Clipper for Kanila.
he said he had also been advised by the
Hongkong Government to take off from longkong as quickly as possi-
ble. He did not know the reason for either of these two mess-
ages and asked my opinion.
I told him I could not imagine what
was back of it but considered Hongkong, in case of trouble, more
dangerous than Manila and suggested he drop his passengers
and
take off.
About five or ten minutes later, he called me again and
Informed me that he had just been advised that Japan had declared
war on Great Britain and America.
I told him that in that case
we would certainly have trouble and that it would be necessary
to get all the planes out of longkong. I suggested that that even-
ing, after dark, he Ily the Clipper to Kunming, where it could be
landed on the lake, and that CNAC would be glad to furnish a pilot
who knew the country and the lake to accompany him.
I packed a suitcase as quickly as possible and drove
into Hongkong from Repulse Bay at once. When I got to Hongkong,
My car was stopped several times by air raid wardens but I insist-
ed on going through and got past them. when I arrived at the of-
fice, I tried to get Kaitak Airport over the phone but could not.
I then decided to go over to Kaltak as quickly as possible. I
went to Star Ferry and found it was not running because of the
raid.
The regulations during the first day, honday, apparently
prohibited anything from moving during air raid periods.
I. then
tried to hire one of the small motor boats to take me over,
but
they also refused to go. I ran into a Police Sargeant, who said
he had to go to Kowloon and suggested to him that we go together,
but he said the boats could not go until after the air raid re-
lease had sounded.
cnego. He said this was against regulations and he might be de-
moted. I told him I thought that would be an excellent idea and
left him. I then encountered a Canadian officer and three sold-
¿ers who were anxious to get to Kowloon. We teamed up and they
forced a sampan to take us over. we got over without difficulty.
There were no Japanese planes visible during our trip.
Arriving in Kowloon, I was fortunate enough to get a
taxi and went at once to the Peninsula Hotel.
There I learned
that the Clipper had been destroyed. Also three Condors,
DC-2's and two of Eurasia's Junkers.
The Clipper crew had re-
turned to the Peninsula Hotel by that time. I got back into my

-2-
taxi and proceeded to Kaitak at once.
On arriving, I found Sharp,
Soldinski, Angle, Schuler, Price, Kessler and Scott very busy
getting the remaining planes off
the field and scattered. There
was no American on CNAC's staff at the Airport at the time the
raid was on and while the planes were being destroyed.
Several
of them started for Kaitak when the alarm was sounded but were
stopped by the police and air raid wardens.
We got all the planes
off the field and on the road,
spaced about 300 yards apart, when
the air raid alarm sounded again.
As there is practically
no
warning in Hongkong, we all scattered. Sharp, Price and myself
and most of the Americans got in cars and drove to the foot of the
hills where we waited.
After about 15 minutes nothing happened,
so we decided to go back, although the alarm was still on.
We looked the situation over and decided the only place
we could hide the planes was to push them off the road onto the
little vegetable patches along the road opposite the Airport and
camouflage them the best we could. It required some grading and
levelling to get the planes off the road, but everybody went to
work and
we pressed in as many coolies as we could.
In about two
hours we had all the planes camouflaged, at least the best we could
under the circumstances.
All we could
do then was to wait for
darkness and hope for the best.
About this time I received a message from Dr. Kung, ask-
ing me to get his family out of Hongkong.
~ I also received several
other urgent messages instructing us what to do at once, but all
obviously written without any knowledge whatever of what the condi-
tions in Hongkong were or might be. I tore them all up.
We then went to work preparing the various spare parts
and supplies for evacuation. As I
was anxious to get back to Hong-
kong to see Madame Kung, I got PAA's mechanic, Mr. Maish, to take
me over on the PAA motor boat. We got out from the shore a little
ways and found the water pump on the engine was not working, so
we had to return.
This was about half past one, I think.
as we got back, the air raid alarm sounded again. We went up to
the hangar and
found that all the cars, including my taxi, had
Left.
CNAC had one truck and we loaded it as full as possible with
our Chinese personnel who were on the field. I sent them away from
the Airport.
There were to Chinese mechanics and myself left who
were unable
to get on the truck. I told them to leave the Airport
and get into a culvert across the road from the Airport.
There was
a big culvert on the Airport,
so I decided to stay close to it and
lf the raid came over - and it appeared to be heading for the Air-
port - I would get into it. Just then Moss came by in his car and.
suggested that we go over to the gateman's office at the corner of
the Airport. It had been sandbagged all around the sides,
so that
It offered good protection except from a direct hit. I got in
with Moss and we drove over to this office at the entrance gate.
By this time two machine guns had been set up on tripods for anti-
aircraft work and were manned by Indian troops. There were two
English soldiers with rifles, including a sargeant, at the gate
and several of Mr. Moss' staff.
Shortly after this, planes began to come over in many
groups and proceeded to fly over Hongkong and Kowloon. There was
20012112720

-3.
considerable anti-aircraft fire but there were also considerable
broken clouds, so I did not see any hits. One raid came over the
Airport about
2 o'clock and dropped bombs. We could hear them
swishing down and we all flopped inside the house, but none of
them came closer than 300 yards.
They all hit around the edge of
the field and across the road.
The Indian soldiers, I would like
to add, were splendid.
They only got one chance to
shoot and that
was not very close, but they stuck to their guns and none of them
flopped when the bombs came.
About 10 minutes to 3, another formation came over the
Airport,
very high up.
They undoubtedly were bombing the Airport.
We could hear the bombs coming again and closer, and again we all
flopped in the house. Eight bombs landed on the Airport and one
went through the hangar which proved to be a dud. It hit the
aileron on one of the Junkers and landed on the concrete floor of
the hangar, breaking to pieces; however, it did not explode.: This
apparently was the last group of the raid, and shortly after this
the release sounded.
Moss and I went out to see the holes and found they were:
all of. little importance. We did not know a dud had bit the hangar
until we went inside and found the broken casing and the H.E.3-
scattered all over the floor. It appeared to be about a 250 pound
bomb.
Moss and I examined it carefully, which proved to be a mis
take as I got some picric acid on my hands and shoes and other
parts of my clothing, turning them yellow. However I did not seem
to be particularly allergic to this and It did not affect me much.
One of our mechanics did the same thing and got some acid on his
face. He turned out to be particularly allergic to it, and the
next morning he was the worst looking object you almost ever
He looked as though he had a bad case of poison ivy all over his
lace •
He got medical attention in Chungking and it soon cleared
Apparently I also got some in ny throat, as I developed that
night a vero bad con, althou to now bad to reced
medical attention in Chungking also It is well now.
I stayed at the Airport until about 5 o'clock and then
one to see Mase Kung whom arred at to fero, arco ong
ered no one
could go over to Hongkong from Kowloon without a police
permit, which I did not have.. So I then returned to the Airport.
At 7 o'clock our first plane,
a DC-3, took off for Namyung, loaded
with CNAC staff and their Tamiliee.
Frank Higgs was pilot. The
second DC-3 took off at 7:15 p.m. with H. A. Sweet as pilot.
•The
DC-2 developed a little radio trouble and did not get off until s-
7:45. These all were loaded. with CNAC staff and their families, a
and
supplies.
I, told her I
At 9:30 I got wadame Kung over the telephone in Hongkong:
had a message from Dr. Kung. I should state here
that
this was the second time that day that I had talked with her over
the phone.
• I told Madame Kung that we had our planes in operation
Fand that we thought we would be able to get her and her family out.
She again raised the question as to how dangerous this would be.
I told her there was undoubtedly some danger connected with it but
I had no way of telling whether this would be more dangerous than

- 4-
staying. As it was then too late for her to get to Kaitak that
night anyway, I suggested that we wait and see how operations
proceeded that night; 11 everything went alright, I would call
her the next day and we would discuss the matter further. This
was agreed.
As everything was then going smoothly, I drove up to the
Peninsula Hotel in the most complete blackout you could imagine.
It was a very difficult job in itselt.
The purpose of my trip was
to see as many Government officials and important Chinese that I
could who might be able to leave quickly.
I saw Mr. Loy Chang and
Mr. Hsi Teh Mou, of the Central Bank, and told them we would evacu-
ate them and their families that night if they could go. Mr. Loy
Chang said he was unable to leave that night and Mr. Mou was
Mr. Mou took me up to Mr. Fox's room; Er. Fox is head of
the Stabilization Board. I told Mr. Fox that we would be able to
take out eight people that night, provided they could be at the Air-
port, bringing 10 kilograms of baggage each.
lir. Ko P. Chen was
there also with Mr. Fox and I told him wa could take him and his
wife, included in this eight. Mr. Fox said he would l1ke to send
of his staff, particularly ir. rese,
whose wife had just had
a baby, and iir. Taylor, also of the Stabilization Board. I told
him uit would take any eight but they must be prepared; I would noti-
fy them later.
I then left to return to the Airport, picking up my secre-
tary, Mrs. Young, on the way and taking her to
the Airport. Short-
iy after my return, Pilot Higgs came in from his first trip to Nam-
yung. He was mistaken for a Japanese plane and the air raid alarm
was sounded and the search lights were turned on. However, Higgs
turned on his cabin lights, so no one shot at him and the release
Fas soon sounded. For a short while, however, it caused consider-
able excitement on the field and a panic among some of the people.
The Standard 01l Company employees, who were operating the gasoline
rucks, gassing our planes,
ran off and never came back. We had to
ges the planes ourselves all night by hand, which caused consider-
able delay.
Shortly after Higgs' arrival, Kessler came in from his
'irst trip to Namyung in the DC-2. He reported that Sweet was hav-
ing engine trouble and was unable to get off.
We dispatched both
of these planes loaded with staff, including all of the Clipper
crew except Captain Ralph, these planes making another trip to
Manyung•
I then phoned Mr. Fox to send his party to the Airport
as soon as he could.
About three quarters of an hour later his
party arrived, including himself and two of his stafi, Mr. Hewlitt
and Mr. Adler.
He was unable to get Mr. Frese and Mr. Taylor as
they were staying at the longkong Hotel and could not get over to
Kowlooni He also had Mr. K. P. Chen and wife and Mr. Tsuy1 Pei and
several other Chinese officials.
By this time Colonel aughes,
*itish Liaison Officer, Mr. Hall Patch, of the British Embassy,
Yr. Cassells, of the Hongkong Shanghai Bank, and a very important
Chinese General from the Headquarters' Staff were also at the Air-
port. Pilot lcDonald came in about this time from Kunming with
the DC-3. We loaded all the above mentioned party on this and
enough more to fill the plane.
This plane was then dispatched
about 2 o'clock for Chungking, with Noods and McDonald as crew.

Later the other DC-3 and the DC-2 returned from Namyung and were
dispatched to Chungking, loaded mostly with CNAC personnel and
supplies.
I would like to express my real appreciation for Mr. Fox.
He organized his party exactly as requested.
Also he did not
include himself until he had made every effort to get all of his
staff out first.
but, as stated above, Mr. Frese and Mr. Taylor
were unable to get across to Kowloon that night. Also he tried to
get Mr. Mou and his wife, Mr. Loy Chang and Mr. Tsuyi Pei to go,
all of whom refused except Mr. Pel.
until he had failed to get anyone
else.
I went back to the Peninsula Hotel and got to bed about
5:30 a.m., pretty well tired out, with a bad cough and a game leg
which I took to be a "charlie horse"
The air raid alarm sounded
about, quarter to seven, but I decided not to get up.. The release
sounded in about 15 minutes and in another 15 minutes the alarm
sounded again.
So I decided it was useless to attempt to sleep,
and got up.
I had breakfast and went over to the Police Station
to get a permit to go to Hongkong.
The air raid alarm sounded
again just as our ferry arrived.
on the second day, apparently,
they let the ferries run during the air raid perioå, so I got over
alright.
I went to the office but there was nothing to do there,
and then I went over to the Gloucester Hotel, where Madame Kung
was staying, to see her.
I explained the situation to her and toia
her we could take her out that night and urged her to go. She was
still uncertain as to whether it would be safer to go or to stay,
but I urged her to get out.
She asked me to call her later and
said that. if she left she would have a party of about 15 and would
like to have a plane for her party. I told her we could arrange
this and we would f1ll the balance of the plane with CNA supplies.
I then
went to the American Club for lunch, then I got my
car, which I had left on the street, and turned it over to a garage,
then returned to the office where I
stayed for an hour, during
which time there were many people coming to see me in regard to get-
ting out of Hongkong.
The air raid alarm was on and off constantly
al1 that day and planes were in the air, but apparently they were
bombing the coastal fortifications and the situation was not at
all bad, so far as civilians of Hongkong were concerned. My advice
to all the people who saw me was to move to the Peninsula Hotel and
be ready to go on short notice and we would do all we could to get
them out.
However, practically everyone seemed to think our efforts
were too dangerous
and were afraid that if they went over to the
Kowloon side they might not be able to return to Hongkong, which
was considered a much safer place to be.
Mrs. K. C. Huang came to gee me,
to speak for herself and
Madame Chu Chia-hua.
Insula Hotel, we would get them out that night.
Later Mrs. Huang
came back with a letter from Madame Chu to her husband, which she
asked me to have delivered and which apparently requested instruct-
ions from him as
to what to do.

- 0-
I then returned to the Peninsula llotel, hoping to get some
When I got to my room, there were many memos and telephone
calls, one from Miss Kung• I called the latter and was advised her
mother would go that night.
I told her the plane would leave about
2:30 or 3:00 a.m. and asked the party to be at the Airport by 2.
Miss Kung then asked me if I could take four extra people, not in
her mother's party, on one of the other planes.
Included
in these
was her fiance.
I told her we would but they must not bring over
10 kilograms of luggage.
The telephone then started ringing con-
stantly and there was a continuous parade of people to my room to
see me.
I should add that a half million dollars National Currency,
Company fund, was delivered to me at my room about this time.
Nong had in some way
succeeded in getting it. P.I. left the hospi-
tal accompanied by a trained nurse.
I saw him Tuesday morning and
talked to him Tuesday night over the phone but was unable to get up
to see him.
We agreed he would try to get all CNAC funds in Hong-
kong transferred out in any way he could.
I signed a check for him
just before leaving for HK$100,000.00 to take care of any of the
staft who couldnot get out.
Among those who came to my room was Mr. Loy Chang, whom I
again offered to take off that night, but who again said he was una-
ble to leave.
Also Carl Neprud, whom I told we would be unable to
take out that night but would certainly take out the next night.
I also saw the Belgian Ambassador to China and his wife, who insist-
ed that they be taken out that night. I told them I considered that
they were in no danger and that it was impossible to take them out
that night, as I hoped to get out a lot of Chinese officials who
would be in danger, but that we would get them out the next night.
I talked the situation over with Mr. Schafer, PA's Dis-
trict Traffic Representative.
lie had wired to Kropff, offering to
remain in hongkong but had had no reply. I told him I thought he
should get out and that we would take him. He said he would be at
the Airport that night. I then drove back to Kaltak in Woods' car,
which I had borrowed.
- Again it was as dark as insida of a whale, and
I got badly lost twice, although I had had no difficulty the previ-
ous night.
Inis was probably due to the fact that by that time I was
rather tired. I should add here that all the banks and stores were
closed on Monday and Tuesday and little could be done. In the short
time I was in iongkong I particularly tried to locate Mr. M. Y. Tong
but was unable to do so.
That night at the Airport we of course had to wait until
our planes came in from Chungking, which was not until after 10 p.m.,
so it was impossible for us to make more than one trip each plane to
Namyung and back and then one trip to Chungking before daylight.
Early in the night, mr. woss informed us that the hongkong Govern-
nent intended to blow up the field. the next day,
have to be our last night. We persuaded them to leave a strip 300
feet wide for us to land on and to continue to operate as long as
possible.
Madame Kung and her party arrived about 10:30. Che was an-
xicus to leave for Chungking at once, but i persuaded her that this
21272c

- 7-
was impossible, as in order to do so we would have to lose a trip
to Namyung, which was most important. By this time I began to real-
ize that it would be perfectly useless for me to stay in Hongkong
any longer, and I would have to go somewhere where I could get some
My cough was getting worse, so was my leg.
Hr. Schafer volun-
teered to remain in Hongkong the next day to handle the traffic.
gave him a list of about l0 people that I had seen and whom I par-
ticularly wanted to get out, and Mr. P. I. iong also had a list ol
about 15. At that time, as far as anyone could tell, the conditions
were unchanged, and I saw no reason to believe that we could not
operate the following night. I therefore returned to Chungking that
night on one of the last planes, coming out with Pilot Moon Chin on
Sharp flew Madame Kung's plane out..
We continued to get
word from Namyung that Sweet's plane was still having mechanical
trouble; in fact, we were informed that one of his engines had burn-
ed out a piston.
Pilot Hugh Chen, about 4 o'clock in the morning, took the
Vultee off and flew it to Namyung, although it had no radio. Also
his compass got out of order about halfway to lamyung and he com-
pleted the trip with a pocket compass. Namyung was overcast and
since he had no radio he could not let down. He went on beyond, and
after dajlight he found an opening and came down on a small emergency
field. He located himsolf and then flew back to Namyung by contact.
There he refuelled and continued his flight to Chunking where he
landed safely.
Pilot Scott started out about the same time with the remain-
ing Condor, containing two new G103 engines, one of which we intended
to put in Sweet's plane.
The Condor also had no radio. However,
Scott developed ignition trouble shortly after his take off and re-
turned to Kaitak.
This Condor was one of those siven to Eurasia and
which they had never flown. He got back to Hongkong in time to come
cut on the last DC-3.
When I arrived in Chungking, Sharp and Woods and myself bo-
gan to make plans to send the two DC-3's and one DC-2 that night
(Wednesday, to longkong.
Sharp planned to go back as passenger and
attempt to take the Condor out with the two engines.
However, just
as we had perfected our arrangements, we received a message from
Moss instructing us not to return that night, giving no reasons.
As there were three people sleeping in every room in the
place where I live and I was by then really in need of rest, I de-
cided to go over to the South Bank and spend the night with cHugh,
who was very cordial and offered me a bed and room to myself. As
there was nothing more I could do that day, I went over to the South
Bank and went to bed about 1:30. I had been gwake for over 53 hours
and on duty practically the whole time.
3o When I undressed to go to
bed over there, I discovered that I had broken several blood vessels
in my left leg,
walch was badly swollen.
lay foot and ankle were as
black as your hat and my leg was yellow. I stayed in bed until 8
the next morning, and felt much better.
I returned to the office on the North side, where there was
a great deal of confusion and pressure from all sides for CNAC to
resume service to Hongkong; also considerable criticisms against

- 8-
CNAC for not bringing out moro Government officials and less CHAC
staff. My answer to that was that we brought every official that we
encounterod,
except the Belgian Ambassador and his wife and Nr. Carl
Neprud, who I thought were in no danger, but I had been unable to
persuade officials to come to Kaitak or even to the Peninsula Hotel
where we could get them, which is perfectly true. Except for one
Chinese general, who came to Kaitak himself, I do not bellove we.
would have evacuated any unless we had definitely made all the ar-
on the Al
rangements and got them to the Airport.
This; of course, was due
partly to the fact that no one expected the situation to worsen so
rapidly. Monday and Tuesday in Hongkong were not bad at all, con-
sidering.
As a matter of fact, I am convinced that we could have
got in and out of Hongkong with perfoct safety on Wednesday and
Thursday; however, It is hardly fair to say this since I was not
EARLES
thore.
On Thursday I called on Sir Archibald Clark Kerr, the Brit-
1sh Ambassador to China, and he sent a rush message to the Governor
1 bongkong, requesting
permission for CHAC to come in that night.
later he got a reply irom the Governor authorizing two ilights be-
tween 9 and 12 p.m. We sent further messages to Hongkong requesting
permission to make more flights the following night but got no reply.
At 4 o'clock that afternoon, two of our DC-3's, flown by Pilots
McDonaid and Higgs, left Chungking for Hongkong to make the two
flights authorized. About one hour out of Hongkong they recoived a
message from Moss telling them that arrangements had been cancelled
and instructing them not to come to Hongkong.
No reason was given.
McDonald and Higgs then changed their course to Namyung, where thes
landed and picked up members of our staff left there on previous
flights cut of longkong and returned to Chungking.
That was our
last effort to get into Hongkong.
On Thursday we got word the Japanese had raided Nanyung
heavily and had repeatedly machine-gunned our DC-3 at low altitudes•"
The engines were ruined and so were the props.
Most of the instru-
ments were shot to pieces, the tires, control lines, hydraulic lines,
landing gear and gas tanks. We have dismantled it and got it off
the field several miles.
We plan to bulld sneds over the fusilage
and wings and rebuild it. It will take a long time and we must have
lots of parts from the States. We can do the rebuilding in five or
six months. I can't even guess when we can get the parts from the
States, but one of these days me will have it back in service.
I would like to say here that I have since criticized my-
selt severely for leaving Schafer. I feel very badly about it, but
at the time it seemed the best thing to do and there did not seem to
be any increased danger.
Schafer's conduct throughout was splendid.
He is a good man and could handle the situation very well. I felt
perfectly satisfied in leaving everything to him, but I am sorry
now that I did.
For the last three days we have made flights every evening
to Namyung and back, bringing out supplies which have been evacuated
out of Hongkong. We are resuming our schedules to the extent of
three times per week from Chungking to Kunming to Lashio and one of
